discovers, develops, manufactures and delivers innovative medicines to fight some of the world’s toughest diseases. Harnessing the best of biology and technology, Amgen reaches millions of patients with its medicines, helping make people’s lives easier, fuller and longer. More than 45 years ago, Amgen helped establish the biotechnology industry at its U.S. headquarters in Thousand Oaks, California, and it remains at the cutting edge of innovation, using technology and human genetic data to push beyond what is known today. Amgen is advancing a broad and deep pipeline and portfolio of medicines to treat heart disease, obesity and obesity-related conditions, rare diseases, inflammatory conditions and cancer. Amgen has been consistently recognized for innovation and workplace culture, including honors from Fast Company and Forbes . Amgen is one of the 30 companies that comprise the Dow Jones Industrial Average ® , and it is also part of the Nasdaq-100 Index ® , which includes the largest and most innovative non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market based on market capitalization. The Rhythm of Life Watch Video Reaching Seriously Ill Patients Worldwide We have a presence in approximately 100 countries worldwide and our innovative medicines have reached millions of people in the fight against serious illnesses. We focus on four therapeutic areas, general medicine, rare disease, inflammation, and oncology, delivering innovative medicines to help make people's lives easier, fuller and longer. Investing in Science and Innovation We pursue new ways to do science using tools like AI, generative biology and human data to discover what is not yet known and develop new precision medicines to fight the world’s toughest diseases. Making Medicines Safely and Reliably Many of Amgen's medicines are made through a highly complex process involving living cells. We aim to deliver for "every patient, every time", and we have a long-running reputation for the reliability of our supply chain. Operating Responsibly Making a positive difference in the world is at the heart of what we do at Amgen — and it goes beyond making vital medicines. We also help build a better world by focusing on environmental, social and governance issues that matter most to our business and our stakeholders. DOWNLOADS Amgen Fact Sheet In This Section Letter to Our Shareholders The capabilities we are building across science, technology, and manufacturing are enabling us to move faster, operate more efficiently, and reach more patients than ever before. With a diversified portfolio, strong commercial performance, and a deep and advancing pipeline, we are executing on our strategy to deliver meaningful innovation for patients and attractive long-term growth for shareholders. Read 2025 Letter to Shareholders Mission and Values Amgen strives to serve patients by transforming the promise of science and biotechnology into therapies that have the power to restore health or save lives. Leadership As one of the early pioneers of the biotech industry, Amgen's innovative and inspirational leadership is a core part of our social architecture. Senior Management Board of Directors Scientific Advisory Boards Brand Partners By partnering with organizations that share our commitment to improving people's lives, we're helping bring science to new audiences, strengthen communities, and extend the impact of research beyond the lab. Therapy Areas At Amgen, we are committed to delivering innovative medicines in four key therapeutic areas: general medicine, rare diseases, inflammation, and oncology. How We Operate At Amgen, we are relentless in applying the highest ethical standards to everything we do. Corporate Governance Business Ethics and Compliance Policies Practices and Disclosures Awards and Accolades Amgen has been the recipient of numerous awards and accolades over the years, ranging from recognition of our pioneering science and innovation, philanthropy and corporate social responsibility to our commitment to being a great place to work. Amgen History A biotechnology innovator since 1980, Amgen has grown to be one of the world's leading independent biotechnology companies and has reached millions of patients around the world. Mission and Values Amgen strives to serve patients by transforming the promise of science and biotechnology into therapies that have the power to restore health or save lives. In everything we do, we aim to fulfill our mission to serve patients. And every step of the way, we are guided by the values that define us. Our Mission To Serve Patients Our Values Be Science-Based Our success depends on superior scientific innovation, integrity and continuous improvement in all aspects of our business through the application of the scientific method. We see the scientific method as a multi-step process that includes designing the right experiment, collecting and analyzing data and rational decision making. It is not subjective or emotional, but rather a logical, open and rational process. Applying the scientific method in all parts of the organization is expected and highly valued. Compete Intensely and Win We compete against time, past performance and industry rivals to rapidly achieve high quality results. Winning requires taking risks. We cannot be lulled into complacency by previous achievements. Though we compete intensely, we maintain high ethical standards and demand integrity in our dealings with competitors, customers, partners and each other. Create Value for Patients, Staff and Stockholders We provide value by focusing on the needs of patients. Amgen creates a work environment that provides opportunities for staff members to reach their full potential. We strive to provide stockholders with superior long-term returns while balancing the needs of patients, staff and stockholders. Be Ethical We are relentless in applying the highest ethical standards to our products, services and communications. Trust and Respect Each Other Every job at Amgen is important and every Amgen staff member is important. We attract diverse, capable and committed people and provide an environment that fosters inclusion, respect, individual responsibility and values diversity. Trust is strengthened through personal initiative and by obtaining quality results rapidly. Ensure Quality Quality is a cornerstone of all of our activities. We seek the highest quality information, decisions and people. We produce high quality products and services. Quality is woven into the fabric of everything we do. Work in Teams Our teams work quickly to move scientific breakthroughs from the lab through the clinic to the marketplace and to support other aspects of our business. Diverse teams working together generate the best decisions for patients, staff and stockholders. Our team structure provides opportunities for Amgen staff to impact the direction of the organization, to gain broader perspective about other functions within Amgen and to reach their full potential. Collaborate, Communicate and Be Accountable Leaders at Amgen seek input and involve key stakeholders in important decisions. In gathering input, strong leaders will welcome diverse opinions, conflicting views and open dialogue for serious consideration. They will clearly communicate decisions and rationale openly and in a timely manner. Once a decision is made, the leader and members of the team will all be accountable for the results and for implementing the decision rapidly. As of **Amgen’s second-quarter 2026 results**, the company’s profile is **strong cash generation and a broad commercial base, with the main challenge being to offset older drugs losing ground to biosimilars and pricing pressure**.

### Strengths
- **Scale and strong cash generation.** Q2 2026 revenue rose 10% year over year to $10.1 billion, and free cash flow was $3.5 billion. Seventeen products were running at an annualized sales rate above $1 billion. ([investors.amgen.com](https://investors.amgen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results/))
- **Multiple newer growth drivers.** Repatha, EVENITY, TEZSPIRE, and several newer rare-disease and oncology products posted strong Q2 growth. Amgen reported that six key growth drivers grew 26% and represented nearly 70% of quarterly product sales. ([investors.amgen.com](https://investors.amgen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results/))
- **A potentially valuable pipeline.** Its obesity candidate MariTide is in multiple Phase 3 studies, including studies of weight management and cardiovascular outcomes. That creates meaningful upside potential, though it remains a development-stage opportunity—not an established product. ([investors.amgen.com](https://investors.amgen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results/))

### Weaknesses and risks
- **Biosimilar competition is already hurting important products.** In Q2, Prolia sales fell 32% and XGEVA fell 34% year over year as biosimilars launched; the company expects more competition. ([investors.amgen.com](https://investors.amgen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results/))
- **Pricing and reimbursement pressure.** Enbrel’s Q2 net selling price fell 22%, with Amgen citing Medicare price setting and a higher 340B mix. More broadly, the company says payer bargaining power and drug-pricing policies can pressure sales and margins. ([investors.amgen.com](https://investors.amgen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results/))
- **Meaningful debt.** At June 30, 2026, Amgen reported $57.3 billion in debt versus $14.0 billion in cash. Its cash generation is substantial, but the debt load can limit financial flexibility. ([investors.amgen.com](https://investors.amgen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results/))
- **Execution and supply risks.** MariTide and other pipeline programs still need to succeed in trials and secure regulatory approval. Amgen also identifies reliance on a small number of manufacturing sites—including its major commercial facility in Puerto Rico—as a potential vulnerability. ([investors.amgen.com](https://investors.amgen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results/))

**Bottom line:** Amgen is a large, cash-generative biotech with growing newer products and a promising pipeline. Its key test is whether those growth engines can keep expanding fast enough to make up for mature products facing biosimilar competition, price cuts, and substantial debt.

**Why I like it:** Amgen’s business is growing: in Q2 2026, revenue rose 10% year over year, and its six key growth drivers grew 26%. **Bottom line:** I’d consider Amgen for a diversified, long-term portfolio, especially for exposure to established biotech and a growing product portfolio. Taking “the past year” to mean **September 28, 2025–September 28, 2026**, Amgen has mainly changed in five ways:

- **It grew, though not evenly across its portfolio.** Revenue for full-year 2025 rose **10% to $36.8 billion** versus 2024. In Q2 2026, revenue was up **10% year over year to $10.1 billion**. Growth was strong for medicines including Repatha, Tezspire, Uplizna and Imdelltra; older products such as Prolia and Xgeva faced falling sales as biosimilars gained ground. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/02/amgen-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial-results))

- **Its obesity-drug effort moved into large-scale testing.** Amgen’s investigational drug MariTide is now being studied in multiple Phase 3 trials—not just for weight loss, but also cardiovascular outcomes, heart failure and sleep apnea. Amgen said more Phase 3 studies in people with type 2 diabetes were planned for 2026. It remains investigational, not an approved medicine. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/08/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results))

- **Some medicines gained new uses or broader availability.** Uplizna received U.S. approval for generalized myasthenia gravis in December 2025 and European approval in February 2026; it also gained a European indication for IgG4-related disease in November 2025. In June 2026, the EU approved Imdylltra for certain adults with extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. In September, the FDA shortened the recommended monitoring time for patients’ first two Imdelltra infusions from 22–24 hours to 6–8 hours, with follow-up assessment still required. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2025/12/fda-approves-uplizna-for-adults-with-generalized-myasthenia-gravis))

- **It expanded manufacturing and added an oncology company.** Amgen announced nearly **$2 billion in U.S. manufacturing investment over the year**, including a further $300 million in May 2026. In January, it acquired UK-based Dark Blue Therapeutics in a deal valued at up to $840 million, adding experimental oncology drug technology. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/05/amgen-announces-additional-300-million-us-manufacturing-investment-totaling-nearly-2-billion-over-the-last-year))

- **Its senior leadership and R&D structure shifted.** CFO Peter Griffith announced his retirement, with Thomas Dittrich named as his successor effective September 1, 2026. CTO David Reese also announced his retirement; Amgen reorganized leadership around research and development, AI and data, with James Bradner taking that combined role. ([amgen.com](https://www.amgen.com/newsroom/press-releases/2026/05/amgen-announces-retirement-of-chief-financial-officer-peter-griffith?utm_source=openai))

**Bottom line:** Amgen looks larger and more focused on growth medicines, late-stage pipeline work—especially MariTide—and U.S. manufacturing. At the same time, it faces erosion in some established products and is investing heavily to build its next wave of growth.

It depends on what you mean by “value”:

- **Health impact:** Patients who benefit from Amgen’s medicines—especially when a treatment addresses a serious condition and improves their outcomes—get the most direct value.
- **Financial value:** Amgen and its shareholders capture the company’s financial returns. But the money is shared across the drug supply chain: in 2025, Amgen’s sales deductions—including rebates, chargebacks and discounts—were 54% of gross product sales. ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/318154/000031815426000010/amgn-20251231.htm))

So, **patients get the clearest human value; shareholders get the clearest financial value**. There isn’t one objective “biggest winner” unless you specify which kind of value you mean.

The **best business growth strategy** is usually not “do more marketing.” It’s to find the most profitable way to attract the right customers, keep them, and increase the value you provide.

### 7 strategies worth prioritizing

1. **Focus on a specific, valuable customer.** Identify who buys most readily, gets the most value, and is profitable to serve. Research their needs and competitors before expanding into new markets. ([sba.gov](https://www.sba.gov/es/guia-de-negocios/planifique-su-empresa/investigacion-de-mercado-y-analisis-competitivo?_ga_F29MXKREMB=GS1.1.1731974400.1.1.1731974400.60.0.682278011&utm_source=openai))

2. **Retain and grow existing customers.** Improve onboarding and service, follow up after purchases, and offer relevant upgrades or complementary products. Track repeat purchases, cancellations, and revenue from existing customers—not just new leads. ([mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/growth-marketing-and-sales/our-insights/experience-led-growth-a-new-way-to-create-value?utm_source=openai))

3. **Build a repeatable sales process.** Map how prospects discover you, decide to buy, and become customers. Improve the weakest step—such as slow follow-up, unclear pricing, or a confusing checkout—before simply buying more ads.

4. **Create a referral system.** Ask satisfied customers for referrals at a natural moment, make it easy to refer, and track how many referred prospects become paying customers. The SBA recommends making referral requests part of the sales process. ([sba.gov](https://www.sba.gov/blog/2017/2017-04/10-ways-get-new-customers/?utm_source=openai))

5. **Test pricing and packaging.** Try clearer service tiers, bundles, subscriptions, or a premium option. Compare results by **profit**, not just sales volume, and avoid discounting so heavily that each new customer loses money.

6. **Choose a few marketing channels and measure them.** Test channels that fit your audience—such as search, email, local partnerships, events, or social media. Keep the ones that bring in profitable customers; stop or revise the ones that don’t.

7. **Expand only after the core business works.** New locations, products, or markets can help, but first check demand, costs, capacity, and the competitive landscape. The SBA recommends grounding growth plans in market research and a clear competitive advantage. ([sba.gov](https://www.sba.gov/es/guia-de-negocios/planifique-su-empresa/investigacion-de-mercado-y-analisis-competitivo?_ga_F29MXKREMB=GS1.1.1731974400.1.1.1731974400.60.0.682278011&utm_source=openai))

### A practical 90-day starting plan

- **Weeks 1–2:** Review sales, margins, repeat purchases, and customer feedback. Identify your most profitable customer group.
- **Weeks 3–6:** Pick one constraint—too few leads, low conversion, weak retention, or low average order value—and run one focused experiment.
- **Weeks 7–12:** Keep what improves profitable growth, refine or drop what doesn’t, then test the next constraint.

Track a small dashboard: **revenue, gross profit, lead-to-sale conversion, customer acquisition cost, repeat-purchase or retention rate, and referrals**.

If you share your **industry, business size, and biggest growth obstacle**, I can tailor this into a more specific plan.

## Practical growth strategies for a small business

The best strategy depends on your industry, margins, and goals—but most businesses can start with these fundamentals:

1. **Focus on a specific customer and problem.** Talk to current and lost customers, review competitors, and identify what customers value enough to pay for. Use that insight to clarify what makes your business different. ([sba.gov](https://www.sba.gov/es/guia-de-negocios/planifique-su-empresa/investigacion-de-mercado-y-analisis-competitivo?_ga_F29MXKREMB=GS1.1.1731974400.1.1.1731974400.60.0.682278011&utm_source=openai))

2. **Get more from existing customers.** Encourage repeat purchases with follow-ups, useful reminders, loyalty perks, subscriptions, or complementary products and services. Ask satisfied customers for reviews and referrals.

3. **Improve your offer and pricing.** Test bundles, service tiers, minimum order sizes, or premium options. Before discounting, check whether the price still covers costs and leaves a healthy profit.

4. **Choose a few marketing channels and measure them.** For example, test local search, email, social media, partnerships, or targeted ads—then track which ones bring in *profitable* sales. The SBA recommends setting marketing goals, budgeting, and comparing marketing costs with the revenue they generate. ([sba.gov](https://www.sba.gov/counseling/manage-your-business/?utm_source=openai))

5. **Make sales easier.** Simplify how customers inquire, book, buy, and pay. Follow up promptly with leads, make your next step clear, and note where potential customers drop off.

6. **Build partnerships.** Team up with complementary local businesses, professional associations, or community organizations to reach customers through referrals or joint promotions.

7. **Protect cash flow while growing.** Forecast money coming in and going out, review expenses, and understand your break-even point before hiring, buying equipment, or expanding. Growth can strain cash if costs arrive before revenue. ([sba.gov](https://www.sba.gov/counseling/plan-your-business/?utm_source=openai))

8. **Expand only after the model is working.** Before adding a location, product line, or major expense, estimate the new market’s demand, costs, and likely revenue. The SBA advises updating the marketing plan and checking financial readiness before expanding. ([sba.gov](https://www.sba.gov/counseling/grow-your-business/?utm_source=openai))

### A simple 30-day starting plan

- **Week 1:** Choose one growth goal, such as more repeat purchases or more qualified leads.
- **Week 2:** Ask 5–10 customers what made them choose you and what would make them return.
- **Week 3:** Test one change—such as a follow-up offer, referral request, or new package.
- **Week 4:** Review results and decide whether to keep, change, or stop the test.

Track a small set of numbers monthly: **sales, gross profit, repeat-customer rate, leads, conversion rate, and cash available.**

If you’re in the U.S., the **SBA’s Small Business Development Centers** offer one-on-one counseling, and **SCORE** offers free mentoring—useful if you want help choosing a strategy for your particular business. ([sba.gov](https://www.sba.gov/counseling/?utm_source=openai))

## International business growth strategies for emerging markets

The strongest approach is usually **focused, locally adapted growth—not a single “emerging-market” playbook**. Countries differ widely in customer needs, infrastructure, regulation, distribution, and business risk. Use this framework:

1. **Choose markets with a scorecard.**  
   Compare countries on addressable demand, growth potential, competitive intensity, purchasing power, logistics, talent, currency and political risk, and regulatory complexity. Weight criteria according to your business model; a digital service and a perishable-goods company will rank markets differently. The World Bank’s Business Ready work is one source for comparing business-environment conditions across economies. ([worldbank.org](https://www.worldbank.org/en/businessready/publications?utm_source=openai))

2. **Validate demand before committing major capital.**  
   Test a narrow customer segment, product range, and geography. Interview customers and local distributors; pilot pricing and service models; and check whether customers can reliably pay and receive the product. Treat “market size” estimates as hypotheses until local sales data support them.

3. **Localize the offer and the economics.**  
   Adapt price points, pack sizes, payment methods, language, customer support, and product features to local preferences and infrastructure. Consider lower-cost tiers or smaller units where appropriate, but protect quality and margins. Build unit economics that account for duties, taxes, returns, payment fees, and last-mile delivery—not just manufacturing cost.

4. **Build distribution around local realities.**  
   Map how customers actually discover, buy, and receive products. Depending on the market, that could mean local wholesalers, retailers, e-commerce platforms, mobile channels, or a direct sales team. Where infrastructure is uneven, design for it rather than assuming reliable connectivity or logistics; digital infrastructure and affordability remain important constraints in many developing economies. ([worldbank.org](https://www.worldbank.org/en/results/2026/05/15/bridging-digital-divide-infrastructure-jobs-growth?utm_source=openai))

5. **Use partnerships to learn and scale—but manage them actively.**  
   Local distributors, suppliers, financial institutions, or joint-venture partners can provide market knowledge and access. Vet partners for capability, reputation, ownership, compliance, and financial stability. Put clear terms around territories, pricing, data, service levels, reporting, and exit rights; keep enough direct customer contact to understand what is working.

6. **Stage investment and preserve flexibility.**  
   Start with an export, distributor, licensing, or pilot model where feasible; move toward local production or a deeper presence only when demand, economics, and operating requirements justify it. Set decision gates—for example, repeat purchases, contribution margin, delivery reliability, and partner performance—before increasing investment.

7. **Manage currency, payments, and working-capital risk.**  
   Model scenarios for exchange-rate changes, delayed collections, import restrictions, and supplier disruption. Where possible, match local costs and revenues, avoid excessive customer or distributor credit, and establish a plan for repatriating cash. The right approach depends on the country and your exposure, so get local financial and legal advice before committing.

8. **Make compliance and responsible sourcing part of the operating model.**  
   Assess risks involving licensing, customs, tax, anti-bribery, labor, human rights, and the environment in your own operations and business relationships. OECD guidance recommends risk-based due diligence across operations and supply chains, prioritizing the most significant risks rather than relying only on supplier codes or audits. ([oecd.org](https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/due-diligence-guidance-for-responsible-business-conduct.html?utm_source=openai))

### A practical first 90 days
- **Weeks 1–3:** Shortlist 3–5 countries; compare demand, competition, regulation, logistics, and risk.  
- **Weeks 4–6:** Interview customers and potential partners; verify pricing, channels, payment behavior, and operating costs.  
- **Weeks 7–10:** Run a limited pilot in one segment or region; track acquisition cost, repeat purchase, gross margin, collections, and delivery performance.  
- **Weeks 11–13:** Decide whether to stop, adjust, or scale—and specify the evidence required for the next investment.

**Key principle:** expand country by country, with local evidence and clear investment gates. If you share your industry, target region, and whether you sell B2B or B2C, I can tailor this into a market-entry plan.

Which options are appropriate depends on the exact diagnosis and medical history.

- **FDA’s Purple Book** — search FDA-licensed biologic medicines, including biosimilars. **Drugs@FDA** has approval information and drug labels. - **ClinicalTrials.gov** — search for studies by condition and location. Discuss any possible trial with the treating clinician; a study listing alone does not mean its treatment is FDA-approved or suitable for you. **Short version:** Amgen is the diversified, established biotech in this group. Novartis and Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) are larger by revenue, while Vertex is smaller but more focused and has had faster recent growth. They’re not perfect apples-to-apples comparisons: their drug portfolios and exposure to patent competition differ substantially.

### Business and scale

| Company | 2025 revenue | What chiefly distinguishes it |
|---|---:|---|
| **Amgen** | **$36.8B** | Broad biotech portfolio across areas such as oncology, inflammation, bone health, cardiovascular disease and rare disease. |
| **Vertex** | **$12.0B** | A highly profitable specialist, still centered on cystic-fibrosis medicines, while building businesses in gene therapy, pain and kidney disease. |
| **Novartis** | **$54.5B** | The largest of these by reported 2025 revenue; a global innovative-medicines company spanning oncology, immunology, neuroscience and cardiovascular/renal/metabolic disease. This is continuing-operations revenue, after the Sandoz separation. |
| **BMS** | **$48.2B** | Large biopharma with major franchises in cancer, cardiovascular disease and immunology, including Eliquis and Opdivo. |

Sources: company 2025 results for Amgen, Vertex, Novartis and BMS. ([investors.amgen.com](https://investors.amgen.com/static-files/2ed3b537-87f5-418f-a22e-c4738cba9a3f?utm_source=openai))

### What recent results suggest

In **Q2 2026**, revenue grew **10% at Amgen**, **12% at Vertex**, **3% at Novartis in U.S. dollars** (1% at constant currency), and **6% at BMS** (5% excluding foreign exchange). Those are one-quarter comparisons—not a forecast—but they show Amgen and Vertex growing faster in that period, while Novartis was feeling more pressure from generic competition. ([investors.amgen.com](https://investors.amgen.com/news-releases/news-release-details/amgen-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results/?utm_source=openai))

### How Amgen stacks up

- **Versus Vertex:** Amgen is much larger and more diversified; Vertex has been growing faster recently but remains more dependent on its cystic-fibrosis franchise. Vertex reported $3.2B in CF product revenue in Q2 2026, out of $3.33B total revenue. ([news.vrtx.com](https://news.vrtx.com/news-releases/news-release-details/vertex-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results?utm_source=openai))
- **Versus Novartis:** Amgen is smaller, but its portfolio is also substantial. Novartis has greater global scale and a broad set of innovative-medicine franchises; a key near-term issue is generic pressure, including on Entresto. ([novartis.com](https://www.novartis.com/news/media-releases/novartis-delivered-sales-growth-q2-and-further-advanced-pipeline-full-year-guidance-reaffirmed?utm_source=openai))
- **Versus BMS:** Amgen is smaller by revenue, but BMS has larger blockbuster franchises and is working through the challenge of replacing revenue from mature products as competition and patent expirations weigh on them. Amgen also faces competition—its Q2 2026 results, for example, showed falling Prolia and Xgeva sales amid biosimilar launches. ([bms.com](https://www.bms.com/investors/financial-reporting/key-facts.html?utm_source=openai))

**Bottom line:** Amgen sits between the larger, broader Novartis and BMS businesses and the smaller, more concentrated Vertex. Its attraction is a broad portfolio and recent growth; its trade-offs include established products facing biosimilar pressure and meaningful debt—Amgen reported **$57.3B of debt** at June 30, 2026. If you’re asking as an investor, comparing valuation, dividends and patent-expiration exposure would be the next step; company size alone doesn’t tell you which stock is the better buy. ([investors.amgen.com](https://investors.amgen.com/static-files/654f0303-beb9-49f5-a91e-37b3f0bb4dd6?utm_source=openai))

1. **Focus on your best-fit customers.** Identify who buys most often, is most profitable, and is easiest to serve. Learn what they value, then sharpen your offer and messaging for them. 3. **Improve your sales process.** Track where potential customers drop off: finding you, asking for a quote, booking, or completing a purchase. Test a clearer offer, faster response times, stronger testimonials, or a simpler checkout. Measure conversion rates so you can tell what actually helps.

4. **Review pricing and product mix.** Check whether your prices reflect the value customers receive and your costs. Test bundles, premium options, or a lower-cost entry offer; avoid blanket discounts that boost sales but hurt profit.

5. **Choose a few marketing channels and test them.** Ask customers how they found you, then focus on channels that reach similar prospects—such as local search, email, content, events, paid ads, or partnerships. The **best business growth strategy** is usually not “do more marketing.” It’s to find the few moves that bring in the *right* customers profitably—and make them more likely to buy again.

### Strategies that work across many businesses

1. **Focus on a specific customer and problem.**  
   Identify your most profitable customer segment and what they value most. Use customer conversations and competitor research to sharpen your offer; the SBA recommends researching demand, market size, pricing, and competition. ([sba.gov](https://www.sba.gov/es/guia-de-negocios/planifique-su-empresa/investigacion-de-mercado-y-analisis-competitivo?_ga_F29MXKREMB=GS1.1.1731974400.1.1.1731974400.60.0.682278011&utm_source=openai))

2. **Grow revenue from existing customers.**  
   Improve the post-sale experience, follow up, offer relevant add-ons or repeat-purchase options, and make referrals easy. Retention and repeat purchases can be a better growth bet than continually paying to replace customers.

3. **Build one dependable customer-acquisition channel at a time.**  
   Test referrals, partnerships, targeted outreach, local search, content, or paid ads. Track which channel produces *profitable* customers—not just clicks or leads. SCORE recommends making acquisition a consistent system rather than relying on one-off efforts. ([score.org](https://www.score.org/finding-new-customers/?utm_source=openai))

4. **Improve your offer and pricing.**  
   Make the value clear, then test packaging, bundles, or good/better/best options. Avoid discounting by default; discounts can lift sales while weakening margins. ([hbr.org](https://hbr.org/2018/09/the-good-better-best-approach-to-pricing?utm_source=openai))

5. **Make selling easier.**  
   Review where prospects drop off: slow responses, confusing proposals, too many steps, or unclear next actions. Set a follow-up routine and measure lead-to-sale conversion.

6. **Remove bottlenecks before expanding.**  
   Document repeatable processes, automate low-value admin, and check whether your team and cash flow can support more demand. Before entering a new location or market, update your marketing plan and forecast the added costs and revenue. ([sba.gov](https://www.sba.gov/counseling/grow-your-business/?utm_source=openai))

### A simple 30-day starting plan

- **Week 1:** Identify your most profitable customer type, offer, and sales channel.  
- **Week 2:** Talk with current and lost customers; find the biggest reason people buy—or don’t.  
- **Week 3:** Run one measurable experiment, such as a referral offer, a new package, or targeted outreach.  
- **Week 4:** Review results and keep, change, or stop the experiment.

Track **revenue, gross margin, repeat-purchase rate, conversion rate, and cash flow** monthly. Growth that increases sales but drains cash or profit may not be healthy growth.

If you share your **industry, business size, and main challenge** (getting leads, converting sales, retaining customers, or improving profit), I can tailor the strategies to your situation.
